title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

learn.hook: You can melt ghee and set it again, but can you ever 'unfry' a puri? That is the difference between two kinds of change!
points: A physical change alters the shape, size or state of a substance, but no new substance is formed. Examples: melting ice, dissolving sugar, tearing paper.
Many physical changes can be reversed, but not all: torn paper stays torn, yet it is still paper.
A chemical change forms one or more new substances. Examples: burning, cooking, rusting, curdling of milk, ripening of fruit.
Signs of a chemical change: a gas is given off, the colour changes, heat or light is produced, or a new smell appears.
Some events have both: when a candle burns, the wax melts (physical) and also burns (chemical).

example.q: Your teacher adds a spoon of baking soda to vinegar. It fizzes. When the gas is passed into lime water, the lime water turns milky. Is this a physical or a chemical change?
steps: Fizzing shows a gas is being made.
The gas is carbon dioxide; it turns lime water milky by forming a new substance.
New substances are formed, so it is a chemical change.
example.answer: It is a chemical change: new substances such as carbon dioxide are formed.

learn.reallife: Making dahi from milk, cooking dal, burning a diya and fruits ripening are chemical changes. Melting butter, making ice in the freezer and dissolving sugar in tea are physical changes.

games.title: Change check
items: In a physical change, no new substance is formed.
Only shape, size or state changes; it is still the same substance.
All physical changes can be reversed.
Tearing paper is a physical change but you cannot join the paper back as it was.
Burning a candle includes both physical and chemical changes.
Wax melts (physical) and wax burns to form new gases (chemical).
Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky.
It reacts with lime water to form a white substance (calcium carbonate).
Dissolving salt in water is a chemical change.
No new substance forms; the salt can be got back by evaporating the water.

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
quiz.explain: Cooking forms new substances with a new colour, taste and smell. The others change only shape or state.
steps: A chemical change forms new substances.
Cooking a roti gives a new colour, taste and smell.
Melting wax, breaking glass and freezing water only change shape or state.
So cooking a roti is a chemical change.
Answer: Cooking a roti
quiz.mistake: Thinks any change involving heat must be chemical

quiz.q: Which of these is a physical change?
quiz.explain: Melted butter is still butter and can become solid again. The others form new substances.
steps: A physical change forms no new substance.
Melted butter is still butter and can become solid again.
Burning, rusting and souring form new substances.
So melting of butter is a physical change.
Answer: Melting of butter
quiz.mistake: Does not check whether a new substance is formed

quiz.q: Which sign usually tells us that a chemical change has happened?
options: A new gas or a new colour appears
The object is cut into pieces
quiz.explain: Gas, colour change, heat or light and new smells are signs of new substances forming.
steps: Signs of a chemical change: a gas, a colour change, heat or light, a new smell.
Changing shape, melting or cutting are physical changes.
So a new gas or a new colour usually shows a chemical change.
Answer: A new gas or a new colour appears
quiz.mistake: Thinks a change of shape means a chemical change

quiz.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz together. Which gas is formed?
quiz.explain: The fizz is carbon dioxide gas. It turns lime water milky.
steps: Baking soda and vinegar react and fizz.
The gas turns lime water milky.
That gas is carbon dioxide.
So the answer is carbon dioxide.
Answer: Carbon dioxide
quiz.mistake: Thinks bubbles must always be oxygen or air

quiz.q: Carbon dioxide is passed through lime water. What do you see?
quiz.explain: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form a white solid, calcium carbonate, which makes it look milky.
steps: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water.
It forms a white solid (calcium carbonate).
So the lime water turns milky.
Answer: The lime water turns milky
quiz.mistake: Does not know the lime-water test for carbon dioxide

quiz.q: Why is tearing paper a physical change even though it cannot be reversed?
quiz.explain: The pieces are still paper. A physical change is about no new substance, not about being reversible.
steps: A physical change is one where no new substance forms.
Torn pieces are still paper.
Being reversible is not the test.
So tearing paper is physical because no new substance is formed.
Answer: No new substance is formed
quiz.mistake: Believes 'cannot be reversed' always means chemical

quiz.q: When a candle burns, which part is a physical change?
quiz.explain: Melting wax only changes its state. Burning makes new substances like carbon dioxide and water vapour.
steps: When a candle burns, the wax melts and also burns.
Melting only changes the state of the wax → physical.
Burning makes new substances like carbon dioxide → chemical.
So the wax melting is the physical change.
Answer: The wax melting
quiz.mistake: Thinks everything in a burning candle is chemical

quiz.q: Which of these changes is chemical?
quiz.explain: Bacteria change milk into curd, a new substance with a sour taste. The others form no new substance.
steps: Curd is a new substance with a sour taste made from milk.
Ice cubes, cut vegetables and dissolved salt form no new substance.
So making curd from milk is a chemical change.
Answer: Making curd from milk
quiz.mistake: Mixes up everyday kitchen changes

teach.ask: Gappu melted some chocolate and also burned some toast. Are both changes the same kind? How can Gappu tell?
teach.praise: Chirp! Melted chocolate is still chocolate; burnt toast is a new substance. Gappu sees the difference!
teach.nudge: Is a new substance formed in the change, or not?

revise.summary: A physical change alters shape, size or state with no new substance, while a chemical change forms new substances. Gas, colour change, heat or light, or a new smell are signs of a chemical change.
focus: Sorting changes into physical and chemical
The baking soda–vinegar reaction and lime water test
Events with both kinds of change, like a burning candle
remember: Physical: melting ice, dissolving sugar, tearing paper (no new substance)
Chemical: burning, cooking, rusting, curdling of milk, ripening of fruit
Baking soda + vinegar → carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky
Candle: wax melting is physical; wax burning is chemical
traps: A change that cannot be reversed is not always chemical; torn paper is still paper.
Don't call melting butter a chemical change; it is still butter.

learn.hook: The Iron Pillar in Delhi has stood for more than 1,600 years with very little rust. Yet a bicycle left in the rain gets rusty in weeks!
points: Rusting is a chemical change in which iron reacts with oxygen (from air) and water (or moisture) to form rust, a reddish-brown substance (iron oxide).
Both air and water are needed for rusting. Without either one, iron does not rust.
Rusting is faster in humid places and near the sea, where the air is moist and salty.
Rust is flaky. It falls off and exposes fresh iron, so the iron slowly gets eaten away.
We prevent rusting by painting, oiling or greasing, and by galvanisation (coating iron with zinc). Stainless steel, made by mixing iron with metals like chromium and nickel, does not rust easily.

example.q: Three iron nails are kept: A in dry air (with a drying agent), B in boiled water covered with an oil layer, and C in a test tube with a little water and open to air. Which nail rusts?
steps: A has air but no water.
B has water but the oil layer and boiling keep air out.
C has both air and water.
example.answer: Only nail C rusts, because rusting needs both air and water.

learn.reallife: Iron gates and window grills are painted, bicycle chains are oiled, and buckets are galvanised so they last longer.

games.title: How a nail rusts
items: A clean iron nail is shiny grey
Moist air touches the iron surface
Iron reacts with oxygen and water
A reddish-brown layer of rust forms
Rust flakes off and fresh iron below starts rusting

games.title: Match the object to how it is protected

quiz.q: What two things are needed for iron to rust?
quiz.explain: Iron reacts with oxygen from the air and water (moisture) to form rust.
steps: Rusting: iron reacts with oxygen (from air) and water (moisture).
Both are needed; without either, iron does not rust.
So the two things are oxygen and water.
Answer: Oxygen and water
quiz.mistake: Thinks water alone causes rust

quiz.q: What colour is rust?
quiz.explain: Rust is a reddish-brown, flaky substance called iron oxide.
steps: Rust is iron oxide.
It is a reddish-brown, flaky substance.
So rust is reddish-brown.
Answer: Reddish-brown
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rust with other coatings

quiz.q: Is rusting a physical or a chemical change?
options: Chemical, because a new substance forms
Physical, because iron stays the same
quiz.explain: Rust is a new substance with different properties from iron.
steps: Rust is a new substance (iron oxide) with different properties from iron.
Forming a new substance is a chemical change.
So rusting is chemical, because a new substance forms.
Answer: Chemical, because a new substance forms
quiz.mistake: Thinks slow changes are always physical

quiz.q: Galvanisation means coating iron with a layer of:
quiz.explain: In galvanisation a layer of zinc is put on iron. The zinc protects the iron from air and water.
steps: Galvanisation protects iron from rusting.
It coats iron with a layer of zinc.
So the answer is zinc.
Answer: Zinc
quiz.mistake: Thinks painting is the same as galvanisation

quiz.q: Why does iron rust faster in Mumbai or Chennai than in Jaipur?
options: The air near the sea is moist and salty
The sun is hotter near the sea
There is less oxygen near the sea
Iron is weaker in big cities
quiz.explain: Coastal cities have humid, salty air. More moisture and salt speed up rusting.
steps: Rusting is faster in humid places and near the sea.
Mumbai and Chennai are coastal; the air is moist and salty.
So iron rusts faster there because the air near the sea is moist and salty.
Answer: The air near the sea is moist and salty
quiz.mistake: Thinks heat, not moisture, is the main cause of rusting

quiz.q: Why is a bicycle chain oiled?
options: Oil reacts with iron to make rust
The oil keeps air and water away from the iron
quiz.explain: A layer of oil or grease blocks air and moisture, so rusting slows down.
steps: Oiling or greasing prevents rusting.
The oil layer keeps air and water away from the iron.
So the chain is oiled to keep air and water away.
Answer: The oil keeps air and water away from the iron
quiz.mistake: Does not see how a coating prevents rusting

quiz.q: An iron nail is kept in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Why does it not rust?
options: Oil turns the iron into gold
quiz.explain: Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil layer stops new air from dissolving. Without air, iron does not rust.
steps: Rusting needs both air and water.
Boiled water has little dissolved air, and the oil layer stops new air dissolving.
Without air, the nail does not rust.
So it does not rust because air cannot reach it.
Answer: Air cannot reach it
quiz.mistake: Forgets that air is also needed for rusting

quiz.q: Stainless steel does not rust easily because:
options: It is made of pure iron
Iron is mixed with metals like chromium and nickel
quiz.explain: Adding chromium and nickel to iron makes stainless steel, which resists rusting.
steps: Stainless steel is made by mixing iron with chromium and nickel.
This mixture resists rusting.
So it does not rust easily because iron is mixed with metals like chromium and nickel.
Answer: Iron is mixed with metals like chromium and nickel
quiz.mistake: Thinks stainless steel is pure iron

teach.ask: Gappu left an iron toy outside in the rain and it turned reddish-brown! What happened, and how can Gappu stop it next time?
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Iron + air + water make rust. A coat of paint or oil keeps Gappu's toy shiny!
teach.nudge: What two things must reach the iron for rust to form?

revise.summary: Rusting is a chemical change in which iron reacts with oxygen and water to form reddish-brown rust (iron oxide). It is prevented by painting, oiling, galvanisation or using stainless steel.
focus: Conditions needed for rusting and the three-nail experiment
Why rusting is faster near the sea
remember: Iron + oxygen + water → rust (iron oxide), reddish-brown and flaky
Both air and water are needed for rusting
Stainless steel = iron mixed with chromium and nickel
traps: Iron does not rust with only water or only air; it needs both.
Rusting is not a physical change just because it is slow.
Galvanisation uses zinc, not paint or copper.

learn.hook: Mishri, the crystal sugar many families enjoy with saunf after meals, is made by a process called crystallisation!
points: Crystals are solids with regular shapes and flat, shiny faces. Salt, sugar, alum (phitkari) and copper sulphate form crystals.
Crystallisation is a way to get large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution.
Steps: dissolve as much of the substance as possible in hot water, filter it, then let it cool slowly without disturbing it.
Hot water can dissolve more of a substance than cold water, so crystals appear as the solution cools.
Crystallisation is a physical change: the substance stays the same, only its form changes.

example.q: Salt can be got by drying sea water in the sun. Why do we need crystallisation to get pure salt?
steps: When sea water evaporates, everything dissolved in it is left behind, not just salt.
So the salt has impurities mixed in.
In crystallisation, pure crystals form while impurities stay in the liquid or are filtered out.
example.answer: Evaporation leaves impurities behind with the salt; crystallisation gives pure crystals.

learn.reallife: Sugar factories make clean sugar crystals, and mishri is made by slow crystallisation from thick sugar syrup.

games.title: Steps to grow crystals (with an adult)
items: Heat water in a pan with an adult's help
Dissolve sugar or alum until no more dissolves
Filter the hot solution to remove dirt
Leave it to cool slowly without disturbing it
Collect the crystals that form

items.text: Getting large, pure crystals from a solution is called ___.
___ water can dissolve more sugar than cold water.

quiz.q: What is crystallisation?
options: Getting large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution
quiz.explain: In crystallisation a hot, strong solution is cooled slowly so pure crystals separate out.
steps: Crystallisation is a way of getting crystals from a solution.
It gives large, pure crystals of a substance.
So it is getting large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution.
Answer: Getting large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution
quiz.mistake: Confuses crystallisation with other changes

quiz.q: Why is hot water used to make the solution for crystallisation?
options: Crystals only form in boiling water
Hot water removes all the substance
More substance dissolves in hot water
quiz.explain: Hot water dissolves more. As it cools it cannot hold as much, so crystals form.
steps: Hot water can dissolve more of a substance than cold water.
As the solution cools it cannot hold as much, so crystals form.
So hot water is used because more substance dissolves in it.
Answer: More substance dissolves in hot water
quiz.mistake: Does not connect temperature with how much dissolves

quiz.q: Is crystallisation a physical or chemical change?
quiz.explain: The crystals are the same substance as before. Only the form changes.
steps: In crystallisation the substance stays the same.
Only its form changes.
So it is a physical change.
Answer: Physical change
quiz.mistake: Thinks forming a new shape means a new substance

quiz.q: To get bigger crystals, the solution should be cooled:
options: By pouring it on the floor
quiz.explain: Slow, undisturbed cooling gives the crystals time to grow large.
steps: Crystals need time to grow.
Slow, undisturbed cooling gives large crystals.
So cool the solution slowly, without disturbing it.
Answer: Slowly, without disturbing it
quiz.mistake: Thinks faster cooling gives better crystals

quiz.q: Salt from drying sea water is not pure because:
options: Other dissolved substances are left behind with it
quiz.explain: Evaporation leaves all dissolved substances behind together. Crystallisation can separate pure salt.
steps: Drying sea water evaporates the water.
All other dissolved substances are left behind with the salt.
So salt from drying sea water is not pure.
Answer: Other dissolved substances are left behind with it
quiz.mistake: Thinks evaporation gives a pure substance

quiz.q: Which of these is made by crystallisation?
quiz.explain: Mishri is large sugar crystals grown from thick sugar syrup.
steps: Mishri is large sugar crystals.
It is grown from thick sugar syrup by crystallisation.
So mishri is made by crystallisation.
Answer: Mishri
quiz.mistake: Does not know what mishri is made of

quiz.q: Why is the hot solution filtered before cooling?
options: To turn it into a gas
quiz.explain: Filtering removes dirt that did not dissolve, so the crystals come out clean.
steps: Filtering removes insoluble dirt from the hot solution.
Then the crystals that form are clean.
So the solution is filtered to remove insoluble dirt.
Answer: To remove insoluble dirt
quiz.mistake: Does not understand why filtering is needed

quiz.q: Which of these is commonly used to grow crystals in a school activity?
quiz.explain: Alum dissolves well in hot water and forms clear crystals as the solution cools. Flour does not dissolve, and milk and oil do not give crystals this way.
steps: Crystals form from substances that dissolve in hot water.
Alum (phitkari) dissolves well and forms clear crystals as it cools.
Flour does not dissolve; milk and oil do not give crystals this way.
So alum is used.
Answer: Alum (phitkari)
quiz.mistake: Does not know which substances form crystals

teach.ask: Gappu wants to make sparkly sugar crystals like mishri. How should Gappu do it?
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Dissolve in hot water, filter, cool slowly, and crystals grow. Sweet science!
teach.nudge: After making the hot solution, what should Gappu do so crystals form?

revise.summary: Crystallisation gets large, pure crystals from a solution: dissolve the substance in hot water, filter, and cool slowly without disturbing. It is a physical change.
focus: Steps of crystallisation and the reason for each
Why hot water and slow cooling are used
Why crystallisation gives purer salt than drying sea water
remember: Steps: dissolve in hot water → filter → cool slowly, undisturbed
Hot water dissolves more of a substance than cold water
Examples: salt, sugar (mishri), alum, copper sulphate
traps: Don't cool fast or stir; that gives small crystals.
Drying sea water does not give pure salt; impurities stay with it.
